abstract: Editor’s note: This is a piece of fiction. Louis sat in the chair, flannel shirt fraying at the elbows, hands resting on his knees. He made to straighten up here and there, but the weight of his years and the thickness of the summer air kept him bent. The radio was bringing him the news.“Here are the headlines for Thursday, July 18, 2013,” said the woman on the radio. She sounded comforted, like someone who knew she was saying something true. “Today, the city of Detroit has filed for Chapter 9 bankruptcy, the largest municipal bankruptcy filing in American history.” Louis heard all the words and understood some of them, if only for their enormity. “The decision was made by Kevyn Orr, the emergency manager selected personally by Governor Rick Snyder.” What followed were a series of quotes by Orr. “This is a problem that has been more than sixty years in the making.” “There’s $18 billion of debt total. Even if we took $200 million a year out of a $100 billion budget, which we can’t do, it would take sixty-eight years to pay off that debt.”The numbers straightened Louis up, especially the last one. That was his age. It would take the city a lifetime—his lifetime, all over again—to break even. The announcer kept talking, but the voice sunk down into the static of Louis’s thoughts.Eventually a beat broke in on him. It was a basketball, bouncing, leading a lanky teenager who was coming down the street. A long thin arm went up. “Yo, Mr. D,” he said.“Rack,” he said. It was the kid’s name, short for Hatrack, on account of how skinny he was. Louis couldn’t remember his real name. As the kid got closer, Louis heard another beat, this one playing off the kid’s phone, which was stuffed into the pocket of his hoodie. It was a woman’s voice, mournful, singing about the streets of Detroit. “Who you got?”“Nick Speed.”“Who?”“That’s the producer on this song. You probably never heard of him.”“Me?” Louis said. “I haven’t even heard of Eminem.” This wasn’t true. He had seen the movie. He had heard of Big Sean and Danny Brown and Dilla. He was especially taken with Moodymann, who seemed to be in church and on the street at the same time. Nick Speed was a new one. He jotted it down in his mind. He would listen on his own. He thought about schooling Rack on Kenny Burrell and Elvin Jones and Black Bottom and the Flame Show Bar and John Lee and Speckled Red and whatever else. He even murmured Yusef Lateef’s name. But the boy had a basketball in his hands. Louis pretended that he was looking at a bird in the sky and let Rack go with a wave. “You got to get to your game. But let it be known that I like that song. It throws back for sure.”Rack had slowed to say hello, but now he sped back up and got himself across the street. As he got near the playground other boys called to him: “D, you late!” That was the kid’s name: DeShaun. He sprinted the rest of the way, caught a pass, and put up a layup. The rim clanged. That kid better love music because he wasn’t any good at basketball.Louis leaned back in his chair. He felt thirsty but didn’t call for his water glass to be refilled. He knew that he would just get backtalk from Nelly. She was his daughter, his only child. She had been sharp-tongued since she was a little girl and these days she was gentler but could still cut. She was a nurse now. In fact, she was Louis’s nurse sometimes. He let her come over and sit and use up all his internet, though she said that wasn’t how it worked, and in return she measured his blood pressure and blood sugar. Thicker than water pressure and water sugar, he liked to say.A car pulled up. It was a Torino Cobra, souped up with a drag pack, and it was the prize possession of his neighbor, Malik. Malik was a man now, gray in the beard, but for years he had been one of the boys on the block. He had hung out on corners and hooped in the playground and slowed his roll for the neighborhood girls. One of those girls was Nelly. Louis ran him off at first, but he came to like him. Malik was a smart kid, math and science mostly, liked to talk about computers before anyone had one. “You could do worse than a boy from around,” he told Nelly.“I could do better,” she said.Malik went away to college for a year but came home when his mama fell ill. At the funeral Malik told Louis he’d be moving along soon but he stayed. He had a job for a paving company. He would help Louis shovel his walk in winter, always wearing a knit cap that Louis called “a Marvin.”Today was too hot for a Marvin or any hat at all. Malik was sitting in his car tapping on his phone. That’s all people did now. When the car door opened, Louis heard, in the brief seconds before the engine went off, a song. Or rather, a piece of a song, only five seconds, a piano, a snatch of vocal. He should have let it sit but he was still thinking about how he should have talked to Rack. “Hey,” Louis said. “My man,” Louis said. Malik nodded up a hello. “You know that song?”Malik looked around. “Which one?”“The one just playing on your radio.”“Oh. The station said the name. It’ll come to me.”Louis laughed.“What?”“You telling a joke?”“About what?”“That’s the name of the song. ‘Come to Me.’”“Oh,” Malik said slowly. “Well, then, yeah, I’m telling a joke.”Louis laughed again.“That song is a big deal, you know.” This was Malik’s cue to take a step onto the front walk. When Malik was young, he used to stand there and listen to Louis talk for as long as Louis talked. “Makes me feel like I’m back in class,” Louis told his wife Ann. She clucked her tongue. “You think that it’s you?” she said. “If Nelly wasn’t in here that boy wouldn’t last five minutes.” After Nelly went away to school, though, Malik would still come around and listen. Nelly’s wedding didn’t stop him, and her divorce didn’t seem to start him up in any new way. Here was Malik, not even knowing that Nelly was in the house, stepping onto the front walk. “You see,” Louis said to Ann, but there was no Ann anywhere except under the ground.“A big deal how?” Malik said.“It’s Marv Johnson.”“Marv Johnson,” Malik said. “He live around here, right? I think I know Ol’ Miz Johnson. Walk with a cane, used to keep a table at Stanley’s Mannia Café? That her boy?”Louis ignored him. “This Marv Johnson recorded the first Motown single.”“No shit?”“None at all. It was so early that it wasn’t even called Motown yet.”“It was Gordy Records?”“No, that’s later. It was Tamla. That was the name of the label. Berry wanted to name it Tammy, after the Debbie Reynolds character from all those movies.” He reached back for what Rack had told him. “You probably never heard of them.”“Definitely never,” Alan said. Louis had taught movies at colleges around the area for twenty years, but he had never taught Tammy and the Bachelor. He tried to remember what movies came from that same year that had been on a syllabus. Sayonara, definitely. Face in the Crowd, definitely. All the Way Home, definitely. He made a mental note to do that one again, maybe paired with The Odds Against or Nothing But a Man. His father had liked Ivan Dixon, but not from the movie—no one had seen it, not really, even the young scholars who claimed to be experts on Abbey Lincoln or Yaphet Kotto. His father had liked Dixon from the Twilight Zone, the episode where he played a washed-up fighter looking for another chance. He had fixated on it because it was his story too. He liked to tell the family hard-luck stories like the one where he won a car in the Holy Redeemer Fall Festival raffle but misplaced the ticket on the way to claim it. Not a Torino but a cherry Mercury Monterey, four doors, white walls. You had to hear that story with a straight face. If you cracked a smile you’d find out that the old man was still fast with his hands. Louis hated him for that but loved him for the way he would imitate the freighter horns and for his thoughts which put him on the same right side as the great men of the day. “History will move you to a spot where your talents can be recognized,” he told Louis, despite the fact that he refused to acknowledge that his son was capable of anything except what he called “wasting time in circles of thought.” It reminded Louis of a line of dialogue from a movie he couldn’t remember: “Parents and children, mysteries no one can solve because you are either the triggerman or the stiff.” Or was it from a book? His mother had been a reader and passed that down to him—“so you can pass it down again,” she said.On cue, a voice came up behind them: Nelly. “Hey, Malik,” she said.“How you been?” Malik said.“I’ve been. Work’s a little busy, which is why I like to come out here for Old Man Story Hour. Yesterday was Oscar Micheaux. Day before was No Way Out. Day before that was Blue Collar. What’s on the menu today?”“Marv Johnson,” Malik said.“Oh, today is music instead of movies? Why?”Malik shrugged. “The song was on the radio when I was getting out of the car.”“Did you get out of the car fifty years ago?” she said. “I can do the Marv Johnson lecture by heart,” she said. “Local singer, starts out as a teenager, Serenaders, crosses paths with Berry Gordy singing around town, Berry hears a song he likes, gets Marv in the studio, takes a co-write credit for himself, Motown is launched. The end.”Louis nodded. “That’s right. That’s all there is to it.” He gestured to Malik. “You might as well get going. Nothing more to learn here.”“Don’t be so sensitive,” Nelly said. “I’m just saying.” She opened the door to head back inside. “Anyone want anything to drink?”Both men said yes. The day had rounded the corner of the afternoon to head into evening, but it was still hotter than anyone would choose.Louis waited until the door closed. “Who you think is singing backup on that song?”Nelly’s voice came from inside. “Marvelettes,” she shouted.“I’ll say that.”“No, no. She knows better. She’s giving you rope because it sounds like Marv would be backed by Marvelettes. It’s the Rayber Voices.”“Rayburn?” Malik said.“Ray-Ber. Named for Berry and his wife Raynoma.”“Ramona.” He was declarative here.“No,” Louis said. “You’d think so, but she was Raynoma. She taught music even before she met Berry. In some ways she was the brains of those early years.”Nelly was back with glasses of tea. “Behind every great man there’s a woman doing his work for him,” Nelly said. “And here you go.” She held the glass out. Malik came up the walk and took it, but something about the moment pressed on him too close, and he backed away a few steps. Nelly stood there in what was suddenly a zone of possibility, and then she went back inside, smiling a little.The kids on the basketball court were arguing now. Louis didn’t like the sound of it. He knew how quickly things could explode, especially in the summer. People around the neighborhood were buzzing about a boy got killed in a dice game up east on Stringham Court. Malik heard the fighting too, turned toward it, not away. Soon enough it turned into laughter and Malik relaxed back toward Louis.“Anyway, back to the song. Nelly was right but wrong. Marv Johnson wasn’t singing around town. He was managing a record store and Berry came in to check on ‘Lonely Teardrops,’ the Jackie Wilson song he wrote with his sister Gwen and Billy Davis. Marv knew who Berry was and played him an early version of the song. I don’t know how much Berry changed but he believed it in enough to take it on. But he needed money to record, to distribute, to promote.”“How much that cost back then?”“He figured a thousand. But he didn’t have it. It might as well have been $18 billion.” He saw Malik’s confusion. Maybe he hadn’t heard the news yet. “The banks and independent lenders were not of the mind to assist to a young man like that, at least not without terms. Sometimes they wanted a stake in the thing. Sometimes the rates were sky-high.”Malik had come closer to the porch, this time with no Nelly to draw him. Money matters pulled a man in. “So what did he do? Start slinging like BMF?”“Not hardly. He went to his family. There were eight kids, and his parents had set up a fund for them called the Ber-Berry Co-operative. Berry pitched. The family considered. The family granted. But they didn’t hand over the full thousand. They ticked it down to eight hundred.”“They shorted their son?”“They exercised prudence. And it wasn’t just giving. There was 6 percent interest, a repayment schedule, everything”“So what happened?”“It happened.” He leaned back but his voice went forward, stronger now. “January 21, 1959. ‘Come to Me’ went to stores and radio.” He remembered hearing it for the first time. He and Ann had been in his blue Chevy 150. She had liked the song but loved it once she saw a picture of Marv Johnson. He was so fine, she said, that he didn’t have to ask her twice. Louis turned his back on the song a little because of that, which only made Ann tease him more. He hadn’t taken it well. He had gotten drunk one night and run around with a girl he saw before he met Ann. Ann found out about it and stepped out with another man, too. There was so much stepping back then. Nelly knew not one thing about it, never would.“Big hit?”“Medium. Regional. That was as far as it could go on that $800 of fuel.”“And then it ran out of gas?”“Not exactly. Berry by this point also managed Marv, and he got him signed to United Artists in New York. They rereleased the song and snuck it onto the national charts. Now the money began to flow a little. He got three thousand dollars as an advance against royalties, and that money went back into Tamla, in part to buy a place on West Grand and start building an office and studio.”Nelly was back outside to collect the glasses. Malik took another sip, though the glass was already empty. “Did Berry buy the building already?” Nelly said.“Just did,” Malik said.“So that really is the end of the story.”“Do you know what else happened the day the song came out?” Louis said.“I do,” Nelly said. “Cecil B. DeMille died.”Louis jerked a thumb back toward her. “This is what happens when little pitchers have big ears.”“Naw,” she said. “This is what happens when the big pitcher keeps pouring out the same stories year after year.”Malik laughed so hard at this that Louis wondered if maybe Nelly and Malik would end up together after all. Sharks on film
abstract: Shark movies are among the most consistently successful at the box office: the statistics dont differentiate between single and multiple visits by ardent fans of shark movies, but the money that they generate speaks volumes. Sharks are among the most visually compelling and naturally spectacular of all animals. Unfortunately, success in the film industry tends to breed imitation, including the repetition of tropes, which can then become clichés. Some of the tropes of shark movies include a large black shark fin glimpsed in an early scene, foreshadowing attacks to follow; the jump scare, with the shark suddenly and terrifyingly appearing; the myth of the persistent predator, the shark that develops a taste for human flesh; the nerdy scientist who proves himself or herself to be heroic as well as brilliant; and the karmic death, in which a villainous character meets his fate in the jaws of a shark. All of these tropes are of course familiar to students of horror films, which is no accident since shark movies so often cross over into that genre. In this chapter we deal with some of the more successful and influential shark movies and dissect some of these representations to demonstrate how accurate or distorting they are in depicting the true nature of the top predatory species of sharks. We consider some of the many ways in which movies simplify sharks, thereby deliberately distorting public opinion about them, through a variety of visual tropes and schemes, some of which are common to thriller horror movies and others of which are specific to shark movies. We also discuss some of the more successful documentary films that have been aimed at better understanding and conserving sharks, but which sometimes undermine their best intentions, for instance through inappropriate sound effects, music or anthropocentrism.

Jumping Sharks
abstract: On Monday January 20, 2020, just as the Covid19 pandemic was beginning its spread across the nation, fifty-eight-year-old David Callahan left his home in Fresno, California, driving his silver Mercedes sedan. Reports would later suggest that David was agitated due to some “domestic issues,” and that he may have been “using drugs”—though exactly what kind of drugs is never really clarified, nor are his domestic issues.David's first encounter with police came when he was spotted driving erratically, weaving back and forth, and nearly hit a police cruiser. As they initiated a pursuit, Callahan refused to pull over. Instead, he continued driving slowly at around thirty or forty miles per hour while the police followed him. This slow-speed game of cat-and-mouse went on for at least five miles. But when he turned off of W. Barstow Ave. onto Dickenson Rd., heading north toward the river, Callahan slammed his foot on the gas and took off. The police watched him disappear.Callahan wasn't on probation and had no warrants for his arrest; he had no real reason to run from the police. There were no weapons or drugs or alcohol in the car, and he might've only received a misdemeanor traffic citation had he simply pulled over. Still, he ran and kept running fast from whoever or whatever he imagined was chasing him. Without braking or slowing down at all, he hit a dirt berm traveling at what has been estimated to be between 100 and 118 miles per hour and launched his car off the south bank of the San Joaquin River, flying 337 feet over the water, or almost the entire length of a football field, before landing on the north bank.The elevation drop from the south bank to the north bank of the river in that spot is roughly sixty feet, which means Callahan's Mercedes also fell the equivalent of a five-story building in just a matter of seconds. As he cleared the river, the car sheared off the tops of trees on the north side before slamming into the ground, tumbling and rolling, until eventually coming to a rest crumpled on its wheels.David Callahan did not survive the impact.In the interviews conducted at the spot where Callahan's car left the road, both a nearby neighbor and a police officer struggle to explain not so much what happened but why. One news station flew a drone camera down the road and off the cliff, over the river, tracing Callahan's path.“It appears the driver did not make any effort to stop, brake, or avoid a collision and was launched up and over the water of the San Joaquin River,” Mike Salas of the California Highway Patrol said.Any effort to stop.Another officer would admit: “Me, personally,” he said, “I've never seen anything like this.” The look on his face said even more—a mix of sadness, confusion, and wonder—and authorities were quoted in local news reports saying they didn't know if the jump was intentional or an accident.The 1978 movie Hooper, starring Burt Reynolds and Jan Michael Vincent, featured, as its climactic final scene, two Hollywood stuntmen jumping a souped-up and reinforced rocket car 330 feet across a gorge in what is considered to be a nearly impossible and ridiculously dangerous stunt.The current world record for jumping a car—landing it and surviving—is 269 feet, set by the professional daredevil Travis Pastrana in 2009 when he jumped a Subaru WRX off of a pier, over the ocean, and onto a floating barge.I saw Hooper at a drive-in theater in Lawrence, Kansas, with my brother and my father. It was part of a spate of movies, specials, and TV shows in the ’70s and ’80s that glamourized the outlaw daredevil and the Hollywood stuntman. Evel Knievel was the big star of the day, but there were others.The actor Lee Majors followed up his role as the Bionic Man with the show The Fall Guy, where he played an aging stuntman/private investigator/bounty hunter. It was an interesting turn for Hollywood: highly paid actors playing the role of the underpaid, overworked, behind-the-scenes employees of the industry—the stuntmen and women, the extras and grunt workers; but it was a successful turn that banked largely on the sustained popularity of Evel Knievel, the self-proclaimed “King of the Daredevils” and “The Last Gladiator.”There were Evel Knievel toys and lunch boxes and bicycles and motorcycles. He regularly packed stadiums with thousands of people for his performances—which involved him mostly just doing some wheelies and standing up on the seat, maybe a couple of practice jumps, before the grand finale, where he jumped his motorcycle over cars or buses or Pepsi trucks or Mack trucks or whatever had been lined up between the ramps. For one of his early jumps, he launched himself over a mountain lion and some Las Vegas showgirls.Evel started out at places like county fairs or local speedways, but as his fame grew, so did the venues. Perhaps his most iconic jump was the Caesars Palace jump in Las Vegas—in part because of his subsequent wreck and the film footage of his botched landing on the ramp.You can watch it on YouTube and see the whole thing unfold in slow motion. It's excruciating to witness Knievel's body jolted, whipped, and slammed onto the concrete. You can almost feel the pain. You watch him tumble and roll, limp as a noodle as he skids across the concrete in his trademark white leather jumpsuit and you think, first, “That motherfucker is crazy,” and, second, “No way he survives that.”It does seem impossible that anyone could survive such a fall. It looks like a video they would show children about the dangers of riding motorcycles. But not only did Evel survive, he went on to try even bigger jumps and suffer even worse crashes. And instead of deterring a generation of motorcyclists, it only seemed to inspire us all the more. All of this was, of course, incorporated into the legend of Evel Knievel, a story that was quickly becoming both bigger than the man and nearly impossible to sustain. You can hear this in interviews with Knievel when he refers to himself in the third person as “Evel Knievel” and you get a sense that all he's ever been good at is being this persona and he doesn't really know how to be anything else. It seems to take a lot of effort from everyone to keep Evel alive.On September 8, 1974, Evel Knievel attempted to jump a steam-powered rocket over the Snake River Canyon in Idaho. Just take a moment to absorb that fact. Think about the choices he had to make before he strapped himself into that metal tube for what some might have called his “jumping the shark” moment—if the phrase had existed at the time. Evel had boasted and bragged about the stunt for months, though, making grand promises that he was likely unable to keep. Both of the test rockets they launched crashed into the Snake River below. Afraid that he might, in fact, call off the jump, one of the organizers/investors had hired armed guards to escort Knievel from his trailer to the rocket. When he finally launched into the air, the safety parachute deployed prematurely and Knievel narrowly avoided sinking to the bottom of the river and likely drowning when the wind blew him back onto the bank.Almost immediately, people began to speculate that Knievel had deployed the parachute himself, but his story just as quickly became that there had been a mechanical malfunction with the rocket. To hear Knievel discuss it is to hear a man putting in the work to sustain a narrative. In his telling, this ending is the only ending the story could've had. If he'd died, he would've been dismissed as just another stupid stuntman. If he'd made the jump and survived, the feat would've been minimized. So, paradoxically, by failing and falling and—this is the REALLY important part—getting back up to jump again, the Snake River jump was a huge success. This failure allowed Knievel to carry on his mission—which seems to be a mix of anti-drug messaging and your standard motivational speaker lines about how you never fail if you get back up and try again or about how it's better to have tried and failed than to never tried at all, or how you have to ride a rocket into failure if you want to jump a motorcycle into fame.Evel should know. He failed a lot. So much so that he made himself famous for doing so. In one of his very first public stunts, he attempted to leap (on foot) over a speeding motorcycle but only succeeded in taking a helmet to the crotch and was flipped upside down. But all of his crashing and falling and wrecking did little to diminish Evel's star power. Over and over again, he ended up in the hospital with dozens of broken bones or, after the Caesars Palace crash, in a coma for a month. Many of his accidents were due in large part to the fact that he was jumping a heavy street bike as if it were a motocross bike (which is, frankly, very stupid) and it didn't have the kind of suspension that could absorb the immense shock of his landings.1 But none of this mattered to his fans, who seemed to love Knievel even more because he crashed and because he kept announcing his retirement and then changing his mind.We love the faulty hero in America, the failed stuntman who seems—if not immortal—at least nearly unbreakable and either uncommonly brave or stupid or both and who is, by virtue of this mix of vulnerability and recklessness, just like us. Knievel would inspire an entire generation of kids—myself included—to try to jump their bicycles over things and off ramps.Many people credit Knievel as the inspiration for my entire generation's embrace of extreme sports; and while the things they do on motorcycles and snow-machines today makes Knievel's jumps look silly and amateurish, there's no question he was an extreme sports pioneer for Generation X.Knievel was a HUGE star when I was growing up, achieving Elvis-like status, and to read the comments on his YouTube videos is to take a walk down nostalgia lane, with many men, of roughly my same age or a bit older, talking about their love for Evel Knievel and their own attempts at daredevil jumps on their Schwinn Stingray bikes—the very same bike my brother and I used to launch off curbs and ramps in the neighborhood where we grew up.Knievel not only failed a lot as a daredevil, he was—by many accounts—a deeply flawed and often violent man who regularly spoke against the evils of narcotics while clutching a cane flask filled with Wild Turkey. He was always, though, his own best storyteller and the author of his own destiny, a man who became the character he played in public until his body could no longer keep up the effort. And when one man whom he'd worked with on the Snake River jump portrayed Knievel as an abusive drunk in a book he wrote, Evel tracked him down and—still inhibited by two broken arms from a recent crash and assisted by a bodyguard—proceeded to violently beat the man with a baseball bat, all in an effort to preserve and maintain the hero narrative of Evel Knievel.The idiomatic phrase “jumping the shark” was born in 1985, but its origins date back to September 20, 1977, when the TV character Arthur “Fonzie” Fonzarelli jumped a shark on waterskis in an episode of the popular sitcom Happy Days. Frankly, the whole thing was just ridiculous and everyone seemed to know it. Designed originally to showcase the actor Henry Winkler's waterskiing skills, the scene features Winkler wearing swim trunks and Fonzie's trademark leather motorcycle jacket as he launches himself over an underwater “cage” containing a fearsome great white shark.Envisioned as a ’50s motorcycle tough guy turned good, Winkler's “Fonzie” character became a kind of magical trickster figure on the show, always in control, never ruffled, and capable of what was known as “the Fonzarelli fix,” wherein he would smack something that was malfunctioning—often a juke box—with his fist and it would magically start working again. But the shark jump was, for most viewers, beyond his magic, just too far, too much, and ultimately too unbelievable, even for Fonzie. “Jumping the shark” has since come to refer to any similarly pathetic stunt, any desperate last grasp at fame or attention, particularly one that departs radically from the expected storyline and devolves into gimmick or a cliché.2When David Callahan jumped his Mercedes over the San Joaquin river, I had just recently turned forty-nine years old. David was nine years older than me, which means we weren't so far apart—both of us stumbling and falling, spinning and rattling through those years of middle age. He would've been an adolescent during the years when Evel Knievel was jumping and crashing through our collective imaginations. He would've grown up with Evel even if he didn't think about him the way that I did, even if he didn't dream of the leap and fear the crash. We could've both been swimming in the same cultural waters.I of course have no way of knowing Callahan's background or his intentions that day, but we know he was driving erratically. We know the police were following him and we have to assume that he knew this as well. So it comes down a couple of possibilities:First, he was intentionally running from the police and accidentally jumped his car 337 feet over the San Joaquin River.Second, he was intentionally running from the police and intentionally jumped his car 337 feet over the San Joaquin River.It's at least possible (if not likely) that Callahan was trying to get the police to chase him in a kind of elaborate suicide-by-cop scheme. But why? Perhaps he wanted to be pursued and pushed to the edge. Maybe he wanted to do something big. He had to know that Dickenson Avenue ends and the road curves sharply to the east along the river where it becomes Herndon Avenue. Right? He had to know.He also had to know that, if he had any hope of making it, he'd have to hit the berm above the river going faster than he ever goes. So he pressed the accelerator to the floor, pushed his Mercedes over 100 miles per hour, and aimed for the other side. I want to imagine he was smiling at the end, returning to childhood dreams of stunt heroics or visions of flying, as David launched himself up and over the San Joaquin River.I realize it's dangerous and perhaps wrong of me to assign intentions of any kind to someone I don't know, someone who ultimately killed himself doing something incredibly stupid, someone who had what some call a “checkered past,” someone who may have been high on the kind of drug that makes you believe you're Superman and you can actually fly. I honestly don't know anything about David Callahan, and I realize I'm taking the risk of making him sound somewhat heroic or, conversely, like a drug-addled idiot. I don't think he's either of those things. And I don't mean to minimize the tragedy of what happened, nor to paint David Callahan as a better or worse person than he really was. I only write to try to understand why I couldn't leave his story alone, why it resonated so much. Once, during the early months of the pandemic, I drove my wife out to the intersection of two roads, to the spot where Callahan jumped. We stood on the berm overlooking the San Joaquin river below, gazing at the other side, trying to find the scar where he'd landed.“Right there,” I said, pointing across the river.But any sign of his impact had already faded.I suppose, on some level, I admired David Callahan—or at least I admired his stunt. But why? What is it about his story that stuck in my brain-craw, tumbling around, unable to process it completely?I realize how twisted this probably sounds to many people. But this is what I do. I find myself obsessed with a story and I try to understand why.I've already published an entire book inspired in large part by my obsession with the story of a different jumping David—David Villalobos—who'd leaped from a monorail at the Bronx zoo into a tiger enclosure and survived the subsequent mauling to tell anyone who'd listen that he was not trying to kill himself but was, instead, trying to “become one with the tiger.”Everyone said he was but I wasn't so I like to against the narrative. abstract: This protocol provides practical, step-by-step guidance for customs and enforcement officers inspecting shark and ray fin shipments to support the implementation and enforcement of regulations related to the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Flora and Fauna (CITES). It outlines a standardized approach to reviewing trade documentation, conducting visual inspections, identifying species, and determining when genetic testing is necessary. The protocol also provides guidance on representative sampling, selecting appropriate DNA identification methods, and maintaining evidence and chain-of-custody records. Designed for use in importing, transit, and re-export countries, the protocol applies to dried, frozen, and processed fins, including mixed shipments and fin trimmings. It complements existing fin identification guides and national enforcement procedures, helping authorities detect trade violations and collect evidence to support enforcement actions.

abstract: Abstract This study aimed to investigate factors affecting visual outcomes after phacoemulsification in highly myopic patients with cataracts, based on the detection of nanobacteria (NB) in aqueous humor. Fifty highly myopic patients with cataracts who underwent phacoemulsification surgery at The First People’s Hospital of Ziyang from December 2022 to June 2023 were enrolled. Aqueous humor samples were gathered from patients before surgery, and NB were isolated and cultured from the aqueous humor. They were identified using scanning electron microscopy and transmission electron microscopy. The calcium-phosphorus ratios in NB cultures (NB group) and nanohydroxyapatite (nHA) cultures (nHA group) were determined by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy. Cell inhibition was compared using a CCK-8 assay. The expressions of calcification-related proteins, bone morphogenetic protein 2, osteopontin, apoptosis-related proteins, B-cell lymphoma 2 (Bcl-2), and Bcl-2–associated X protein in cells were examined by western blot. Based on the best-corrected visual acuity (VA) 3 months after surgery, patients were classified into a normal vision (NV) group (best-corrected VA ≥0.3) and an abnormal vision (AV) group (best-corrected VA <0.3). The factors influencing postoperative VA and efficacy were analyzed. Results revealed that the characteristics of the aqueous humor cultures were consistent with the features of NB described in the literature, with NB measuring approximately 90 to 340 nm in transmission electron microscopy. Energy-dispersive X-ray results indicated no remarkable difference in calcium-phosphorus ratios between the NB and nHA groups (p > 0.05), but the NB group exhibited remarkably stronger cell inhibition relative to the nHA group (p < 0.05). Western blot results revealed obviously higher levels of bone morphogenetic protein 2, osteopontin, and Bcl-2–associated X proteins in the NB group compared to the nHA group (p < 0.05), while Bcl-2 expression was sharply lower, with a great difference in the NB group (p > 0.05). The gap in best-corrected VA 1 month after surgery between the NV group (68%) and the AV group (32%) was obvious (p < 0.05). With increasing recovery time, the number of patients with best-corrected VA ≥0.3 at 6 months postoperatively substantially increased (86%). The NB-positive rate in the aqueous humor samples was observably lower in the NV group than the rate in the AV group (p < 0.05). Univariate logistic regression analysis revealed great differences in age, duration of high myopia, axial length (AXL), corneal astigmatism, incidence of macular disease, and NB-positive rate (p < 0.05). Multivariate logistic regression analysis indicated that AXL and the presence of NB in the aqueous humor were independent factors influencing the postoperative visual prognosis of highly myopic patients with cataracts (p < 0.05). The experimental results signified that NB cultures suppressed cells and, at the cellular level, influenced the visual recovery after surgery by regulating the expression of calcification-related proteins and mitochondrial apoptosis-related proteins. Multivariate logistic regression analysis further confirmed that AXL and the presence of NB in the aqueous humor were independent factors affecting the postoperative visual prognosis. This finding offered strong support for the future development of relevant treatment modalities.

title: Shark Fishing
abstract: Shark Fishing Allegra Hyde (bio) There was a storm, a shipwreck. There were Puritans looking for a place to pray. A reef—serrated and rising from the sea—named the Devil’s Backbone by those who out-swam the drowning tug of hosiery and buckled boots, the swift darkness in a throatful of brine, who felt the soft footing of a sandy shore. The island they named Eleuthera, a Greek word for freedom. Then there was a cave like a yawning mouth: a home, high-ceilinged, acoustics of the finest church. A rocky pulpit—too perfect for coincidence—a sign to the Eleutherans: a gift from God. The island knelt before them, a blank surface of sea and sky, waiting to be given a past and a future. This is that future: the locals call the island “Lutra,” as if sun and salt could erode letters too. They fish from docks staggering rotten-legged into the sea, their bodies black against the horizon—like human hieroglyphics—and yet, how hard it is to read the meaning in their poses. To separate defiance from defeat. These children of children of children of slaves, shackled and shipped to an island named Freedom. The locals, they speak too quick for me to understand sometimes, their voices like chiming bells. “Dats da ting,” they tell me, dark arms lifting slack fishing lines. “Groupa gettin smalla an smalla.” Before long, the Eleutherans feared they’d failed their maker. The rye they’d planted hadn’t come. Their few spades cracked and split. They sweated, starved, dug graves for their companions. Gripped scripture with cracked and bleeding hands. AFFLICTION IS A BITTER ROOT, BUT IT BEARS THE SWEETEST FRUIT. “Got ’em,” says Nehemiah, reeling in a dripping fish, scales silver. He knifes the belly open, shows me a final rubied pulse. He looks relieved. Remorseful. “Only da old men do da dirty work now,” he says, tossing fish guts off the dock. “Da kids, dey all gone.” The sun hangs low, hammocked by the afternoon. The sea swallows a little more of the coast. [End Page 83] BUT IT BEARS THE SWEETEST FRUIT The Eleutherans begged for help from northern churches, praised God when it arrived—bundled and blessed—on a charitably chartered vessel. They unpacked crates of sugar and salted pork; axes, hoes, and saws; they unpacked munitions and pewter spoons; beeswax candles, starched white linens, and silver sewing needles; they unpacked the makings, or so it seemed, of a bold new civilization. To proffer thanks? The Eleutherans shipped ten tons of Braziletto timber back to Boston. The wood became precious anywhere but on the island. Red-grained, good for dyes and violin bows, its sale endowed Harvard University. I am at the same university hundreds of years later, in a room packed tight with students. I am here to speak of Eleuthera—an island fragment in the spill of the Bahamas—to speak of Camp Hope, our work there, a new era of environmental innovation. I have become like Braziletto: valuable elsewhere. The students shift in their seats. Stare with cautious piety. I shift too, hands braced against the podium, waiting for my words to settle into order, the ones that have ballooned and thickened, made me a new kind of evangelist. “Thank you, I—” But my words, I feel them crowded out. “I—” The Eleutherans. They wander through my mind as if they’d colonized that too. Things disappeared on the island. The Eleutherans never met the Lucayans, a boat-building people who walked its beaches before them, who canoed between coves, gold-cheeked and sable-haired. Who disappeared, some years earlier, when the Spanish dropped anchor and enslaved them all. The Lucayans: the goldest thing Cristóbal Colón could find. The Eleutherans roamed their new home, discovering mounds of picked-out mussel shells, shards of palmetto ware. They found Lucayan axe heads, arrowheads, skulls—eye sockets spilling sand—in the place they’d come to call Preacher’s Cave. The Eleutherans discarded these scraps of the past. Seated in front of my podium, a bone pale girl peers into me as if through water. You’re imagining it...

HOW SHARKS SENSE SMELLS
abstract: The smooth dogfish, Mustelus canis, is a small shark that feasts on lobster, squid, and other small shellfish, finding its food by tracking odour plumes. It doesn't just follow its nose, but also relies on the movement of the water and vibrations, picked up by its lateral line system, to find its meal. Jayne Gardiner and Jelle Atema wanted to know how the dogfish used their different senses – smell, mechanoreception by the lateral line and vision – to track odour plumes in a large flow tank(p. 1925).The sharks had two odour plumes to choose from: seawater or yummy squid juice. Each plume was squeezed out of a small nozzle to create a relatively smooth `oozing' odour source, which became turbulent as it flowed over a brick 15 cm downstream of the nozzle. When the lights were on, and all their senses were intact, the sharks preferred the turbulent part of the odour plume,indicating their choice by biting or nudging the brick. When the team knocked out the lateral line using streptomycin, the sharks had to search for longer,but couldn't distinguish between turbulent and oozing odour, suggesting that they couldn't tell the difference between smooth and turbulent flow without their lateral lines.When the team plunged the sharks into darkness, the intact sharks had no problems choosing the turbulent odour, however those whose lateral lines weren't working rarely found the odour plumes. The few sharks that did find them couldn't tell the seawater or squid odours apart. This shows that sharks need both their lateral line and sense of smell to track odours. If their lateral line is not working, vision can help them to find the source of the smell, but if the lights go out, the fish have big problems, and might go hungry.

venue: Journal of Advanced Research in Fluid Mechanics and Thermal Sciences
abstract: In these days, there are some researches related to bio-inspired shark skin’s drag reduction and antifouling to improve fuel consumption of ships. But the bio-inspired shark skin has a demerit that antifouling effect of skins is lost when they are at anchor in a few weeks. In this study, to add the antifouling effect on the bio-inspired shark skins at anchor, the vibration of the skin is tried to be used. As for the targeted model, real shark skin model is created by using µCT figures of mako shark skin. Flow field around the shark skin is analyzed by CFD when real shark skin or flat skin vibrate. The fluid is water and it is treated as laminar flow. To simulate flow field by sinusoidal vibration of shark skin, opposite side to skin is treated as inlet and shark skin side except for shark skin is treated as outlet. As for the boundary condition for these parts, velocity and pressure are given as sinusoidal wave at the inlet, and pressure is 0 at the outlet. And boundary condition at shark skin and other sides are treated as fixed wall. In addition, wall shear stress on one denticle and two denticles is analyzed. As a result, it is shown that flow field near shark skin is complicated and maximum wall shear stress on the skin increases as frequency of vibration increases. And there is linear relationship between flow velocity and wall shear stress. In the case of vibration of two denticles of shark skin, wall shear stress on the skin is influenced by distance and angle between two denticles. It is concluded that (1) The possibility of adding antifouling effect on shark skin increases with vibration, (2) Wall shear stress on shark skin will be increased by optimizing distance and angle between two denticles in the case of vibration.

Supplementary Material for: Sexual Dimorphism of the Electrosensory System: A Quantitative Analysis of Nerve Axons in the Dorsal Anterior Lateral Line Nerve of the Blue-Spotted Fantail Stingray (Taeniura lymma)
abstract: Quantitative studies of sensory axons provide invaluable insights into the functional significance and relative importance of a particular sensory modality. Despite the important role electroreception plays in the behaviour of elasmobranchs, to date, there have been no studies that have assessed the number of electrosensory axons that project from the peripheral ampullae to the central nervous system (CNS). The complex arrangement and morphology of the peripheral electrosensory system has a significant influence on its function. However, it is not sufficient to base conclusions about function on the peripheral system alone. To fully appreciate the function of the electrosensory system, it is essential to also assess the neural network that connects the peripheral system to the CNS. Using stereological techniques, unbiased estimates of the total number of axons were obtained for both the electrosensory bundles exiting individual ampullary organs and those entering the CNS (via the dorsal root of the anterior lateral line nerve, ALLN) in males and females of different sizes. The dorsal root of the ALLN consists solely of myelinated electrosensory axons and shows both ontogenetic and sexual dimorphism. In particular, females exhibit a greater abundance of electrosensory axons, which may result in improved sensitivity of the electrosensory system and may facilitate mate identification for reproduction. Also presented are detailed morphological data on the peripheral electrosensory system to allow a complete interpretation of the functional significance of the sexual dimorphism found in the ALLN.

abstract: O grupo Batoidea engloba as raias e seu monofiletismo é bem corroborado. Contudo, as inter-relações filogenéticas dentro do grupo ainda são discutíveis. Algumas filogenias consideram Pristiformes como grupo basal de Batoidea, enquanto outras consideram Torpediniformes como mais basal. O grupo dos Rhinobatiformes é visto como monofilético por alguns autores e como parafilético por outros. O grupo dos Myliobatiformes também apresenta problemas em suas inter-relações: alguns autores consideram Hexatrygon como grupo mais basal, outros consideram Urotrygon, além de outras hipóteses para a filogenia deste grupo. A distribuição dos canais do sistema sensorial de linha lateral apresenta grande variação entre os grupos de Batoidea e, apesar deste sistema não ser muito bem estudado em elasmobrânquios, constitui uma importante fonte de caracteres filogenéticos. Dessa forma, buscou-se, neste projeto, descrever a distribuição e a morfologia dos canais do sistema de linha lateral do grupo Batoidea, levantando possíveis caracteres de relevância sistemática que auxiliem na resolução dos problemas filogenéticos neste grupo. Com base na análise dos padrões encontrados em 55 espécies pertencentes a 39 gêneros e 18 famílias de Batoidea e em informações revisadas da bibliografia, foram propostos 13 caracteres, os quais foram discutidos de acordo com questões filogenéticas dentro de Batoidea. Assim, puderam ser abordados problemas como o grupo basal de Batoidea e o posicionamento dos gêneros Platyrhina e Zanobatus, além de discussões acerca do monofiletismo de Myliobatiformes e seus grupos internos

title: A new perimetric color vision analyzer.
abstract: A new apparatus was developed for mapping the extrafoveal color vision, the perimetric color vision analyzer. A yellow test object with varying degrees of saturation is presented on a cathode ray tube color display in a random sequence at one of 10 points around the fixation spot. The background is a mosaic pattern consisting of gray spots of the same size and shape as the test object, with various luminances. Background patterns with or without a test object are presented alternately. The subject is instructed to press a key when he detects a yellow object in the background pattern. The luminance of the test object is in the same range as the background gray spots. Since the luminance of background spots is changed synchronously at random when the test object appears, the subject can detect the test object only by the difference in color saturation. The results show the color contrast sensitivity at every designated point in the central visual field. The clinical application of the perimetric color vision analyzer revealed extrafoveal color defects which could not be evaluated with conventional color vision tests. It also showed that in some chorioretinal and optic nerve disorders the topographic pattern of color contrast sensitivity disagrees with that of luminance contrast sensitivity measured with automated static perimetry.

Species associations and community structure in an oceanic elasmobranch assemblage
abstract: Elasmobranch assemblages support marine ecosystem health by regulating populations, transferring nutrients across habitats, and sustaining high-level consumers. Shifts in elasmobranch assemblages can reshape ecosystem dynamics through direct and indirect species associations. Here, we analyzed a 26 yr underwater visual survey dataset from Cocos Island National Park in the Eastern Tropical Pacific to examine community-level temporal shifts in the island’s elasmobranch assemblage. We studied 13 species, analyzing changes in network strength, diversity indices, and species associations. We show a shift from a sparse, low-richness network in the early 1990s to a more densely connected assemblage by 2014. The elasmobranch assemblage showed 2 seasonal sub-communities: migratory oceanic species in the wet season and resident coastal species in the dry season. Scalloped hammerhead Sphyrna lewini and whitetip reef sharks Triaenodon obesus were the main contributors to year-to-year diversity changes. Significant association model outputs showed mostly negative associations, suggesting that predator-prey dynamics and intraguild competition are taking place in Cocos Island. We inferred 3 types of association patterns: (1) competition, when negative associations were possibly caused by competitive interactions rather than predator-prey dynamics; (2) predation, inferred when prey abundances were negatively associated with predator covariates; and (3) environmental preference, where shared or opposing thermal or seasonal habitat patterns explained positive or negative associations, respectively. Our findings advance understanding of the evolving Cocos Island elasmobranch community structure and network dynamics. Our study also provides a framework for examining the mechanisms driving interspecific associations in similar marine ecosystems.

Swimming among the sharks
abstract: “…Competition is. In every business, no matter how small or how large, someone is just around the corner forever trying to steal your ideas and build his success out of your imagination, struggling after that which you have toiled endless years to secure, striving to outdo you in each and every way. If such a competitor would work as hard to originate as he does to copy, he would much more quickly gain success….” Alice Foote MacDougall (1867–1945), Successful New York City restaurateur Indeed, competition always has been and always will be. Basically, this article is about competing, but it is also about maintaining your independent audiology/dispensing practice while competing with the Beltones, Miracle-Ears, HearUSAs, and other big fish in the hearing care pond. Corporate audiology is growing, no doubt. In the past 11 years, the chains have in-creased their numbers from approximately 900 units in 1995 to about 2300 in 2006. Of that growth, 80% has occurred in just the past 3 years. Why the corporate growth? In a word, opportunity. Right now, America has more than 32 million baby boomers over the age of 50. And, according to hearing healthcare industry statistics cited in this magazine last October, over the next 20 years the number of Americans with hearing loss is expected to increase from today's 32 million to 70 million. Moreover, in the next 5 years alone, 22 million will reach age 50. That is very good news for our industry, and it gives all of us “a big sea” to swim in! Add to those numbers the advantageous facts that consumers are becoming increasingly health conscious and more and more determined to remain young and active longer. They also want to be involved in the process and are used to spending money. Independent practice owners hold many advantages that can lead to growth and success. These include a passion for what they do and a commitment to offering the highest level of care and service and the best value for dollars spent. They are not as driven as corporates by a bottom-line orientation, and they can select the most appropriate product for each patient from a wide range of brands rather than just one. The latter, in particular, gives independents tremendous advantages in the areas of service and marketing. TWO PATHS TO CHOOSE BETWEEN So, you may be wondering, how can the little guy, the solo or two-person practice with just one or two offices, compete successfully with the corporates? First, let's look at two of the possible choices: You could go head-to-head with your competitor, striving to beat it at its own game. Or, you can set and maintain your own course, implement a strategy of your choosing, follow the business and marketing plans that you designed, and fulfill your practice's mission. Going head-to-head If you take this route, be prepared to face some risks. And, be forewarned that if you do go head-to-head with a large competitor, you may be taking an irrevocable step. You also must be prepared to lose. For example, what do you do when the competitor cuts prices? Competing on price is never a good tactic, so do not allow yourself to be drawn into a price war. It is the worst kind of competition in which no one wins, not even the patient. But if you feel you must compete on price, be sensible about it. For example, bundle your pricing and alert patients to price-cut risks. Even consider increasing your prices! That way, you can accept your competitor's coupons. Plus, if someone mentions your competitor's (lower) price, you can consider matching it. Modify your pricing for certain designated products by offering instruments in all price ranges. Select a “fighting” brand, one that has your confidence and that you can price low and still make a reasonable profit. Above all, continue emphasizing the quality of your services and your wide range of products. Raise the level of your customer care. Alternatives approaches At American Hearing Aid Associates (AHAA), we generally recommend that independents not focus exclusively on competing head-to-head. We offer a number of alternatives, and can provide comprehensive personalized support to help ensure an independent's success. We advise independents to stay on course. We tell them, draft your strategic, business, and marketing plans and focus on implementing them. Market. Advertise. Achieve operational excellence. Get close to your patients. Reinvigorate your practice's culture and vision. As you plan, examine your practice and yourself very closely. Do the SWOT analysis. That is, identify your practice's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. Scrutinize your practice along multiple parameters, using objective measures wherever possible. Identify all the products and services you offer. Understand the benefits of each for your patients and potential patients. Determine if you are staffed properly for service and growth, if you have the proper financial base for growth. Involve your employees in the process. Survey patients—and also people who did not buy—to determine their levels of satisfaction with your products and your services. Be prepared to hear both good and bad comments, and make any changes needed to address the bad comments. Identify where your current patients are coming from. Look at your database to see if any areas exist where you are not represented or poorly represented. Make sure that you and your staff are trying to get patients to upgrade older, obsolete instruments. If you think your marketing is weak, determine why. Are you and your staff using the right words? Do staff phone skills need improving? Is your practice too little known? Are you offering patients what you think they need instead of what they think they need? Are you offering so many services that you're confusing prospects? Identify the messages your advertising is sending, and understand how to im-prove the effectiveness of those messages. For example, Rex Briggs and Greg Stuart, successful advertising executives and marketing researchers, have found that an advertising message heard three different times in a single medium (e.g., a commercial you see on TV three times) is far less effective than a message experienced one time each in three different media (e.g., in a TV spot, a print ad, and a radio commercial). The numbers show beyond a doubt that this “surround-sound” approach is best. COMPARE YOURSELF WITH THE COMPETITION After you have examined your own practice carefully, conduct a core competencies analysis comparing your strengths and weaknesses with those of your competitors. Figure out what differentiates your practice from the competitors'. Have you already taken steps to strengthen your market position? For example, have you opened a new office or increased your advertising? Or, is it your competitor who has made this type of move? And what could be around the corner? That is, what scares you most about the year ahead? What one or two actions could a competitor take to hurt you? What mergers or deals could have a negative impact on your practice? And ask yourself, what are your winning moves? What can you do to tilt the playing field in your favor? Should you be considering an acquisition, offering new products, adding sales staff? Finally, identify the positive differences between you and your competitors, and promote them heavily in your marketing. GO FAR OUTSIDE THE BOX! Most businesses focus on matching and beating their rivals in a narrow area. Their tactics tend to converge along the same basic dimensions of competition. As a result, businesses end up beating their brains out in a single-dimension framework. So, how can you compete in a different dimension? For starters, look for substitute and alternative patients. What market is your competitor—and perhaps you, too—not tapping? Find it, then tap it. Here's another question: When the consumer should be buying a hearing aid, what is he or she buying instead? How can you steer them to the advantages of better hearing and make that their priority? Who are the “influencers” in your community? Can you increase your sales to them so they can become allies in your marketing? Intensify your efforts to gain medical referrals. Identify respected physicians in your area and put together proposals for them. Market to them. Start with the doctors of patients you attracted on your own, not through a referral. It is a long-term process; stick with it. CONCLUSION The opportunities for growth in hearing healthcare are great today and will only become greater over the next 20 years. That said, it's certain that corporates will continue expanding to take advantage of the growing base of potential patients. The marketplace is heating up. You have to plan for adaptation and change so you aren't eaten up by the competition. And you have a number of choices. You can selectively go head-to-head, you can do your own thing, you can go outside the box, or you can do any combination of the first three. Challenging times call for bold measures. You can swim among the sharks, so zip up your wet suit and enjoy your swim! “The only competition worthy of a wise man is with himself.” Washington Allston (1779–1843), American artist

title: Automated Visual Fin Identification of Individual Great White Sharks
abstract: This paper discusses the automated visual identification of individual great white sharks from dorsal fin imagery. We propose a computer vision photo ID system and report recognition results over a database of thousands of unconstrained fin images. To the best of our knowledge this line of work establishes the first fully automated contour-based visual ID system in the field of animal biometrics. The approach put forward appreciates shark fins as textureless, flexible and partially occluded objects with an individually characteristic shape. In order to recover animal identities from an image we first introduce an open contour stroke model, which extends multi-scale region segmentation to achieve robust fin detection. Secondly, we show that combinatorial, scale-space selective fingerprinting can successfully encode fin individuality. We then measure the species-specific distribution of visual individuality along the fin contour via an embedding into a global `fin space'. Exploiting this domain, we finally propose a non-linear model for individual animal recognition and combine all approaches into a fine-grained multi-instance framework. We provide a system evaluation, compare results to prior work, and report performance and properties in detail.

venue: Studies in Linguistics Culture and FLT
abstract: This piece of research, which is part of a project concerned with the translatability of figurative language in AV content from English into Arabic and vice versa, investigates the translatability of visual puns in the animated movie Shark Tale from English into Arabic in both its subtitled and dubbed versions. The data of this study consist of the original English film scenes and their Arabic subtitles and dubs. Based on Aleksandrova’s (2019) taxonomy, which treats pun translation as a cognitive game in the translator’s mind, it was confirmed that puns can be translated by accepting the game of translation using two different strategies: (a) Quasi-translation: where the translator preserves one of the signs of the original pun and replaces the other with a suitable one from the target language. (b) Free Translation: where the translator replaces the two signs of the source pun with new signs from the target language. It was also confirmed that the game of translation can be rejected by using Literal Translation where the translator literally translates the pun into the target language. Another minor issue raised in this study is that visual puns and complex puns that are culturally very local are subject to be ignored by No Translation, which is the omission of the linguistic host of pun. The current study concludes by providing some implications and solutions for translators dealing with pun in animated films.

abstract: Underwater sound travels five times faster in water than in air and presents an important sensory cue that is used by many marine organisms for orientation, mating, feeding and territory defense. Sharks and rays have been swimming in our oceans for more than 400 million years and possess inner ears to listen to the many sounds in the ocean but are not historically viewed as active sound producers. Three recent reports of several species of rays producing clicks in response to approaching divers have cast doubt on this long prevailing view and resulted in calls for more research into sound production in elasmobranchs. But how do we know what these animals can hear and what they might listen to? In this talk I will give a short introduction into underwater sound, touch briefly on the impacts of man-made noise pollution on marine animals. I then will give a brief overview of what methods researchers, including myself, use to study hearing abilities and sound perception in sharks. Lastly, I will talk about how I came to discover that New Zealand rig sharks can make strange noises and discuss some of the open questions in this field of research.

abstract: We propose a novel laboratory test of gravity combining seismic-wave measurements with cosmic-ray muon detections. Quantum-gravity corrections to the anharmonic Debye model are derived, yielding a modified bulk modulus that encodes deviations from standard gravity. The usual dependence on density, a dominant source of uncertainty, is removed via muon tomography and seismic velocities measurement. We show that this setup can constrain gravity parameters at a level comparable to current laboratory experiments. Prospects for further improvements are briefly discussed.

Signal Transduction in Photoreceptor Proteins
venue: Gothenburg University Publications Electronic Archive (Gothenburg University)
abstract: The ability to sense and react to different light conditions is of great importance for many organisms on the face of the earth. Specialized proteins known as photoreceptor proteins provide bacteria, plants and animals with this ability. To be able to sense the light the photoreceptor proteins have small molecules, known as chromophores, embedded within the protein matrix. Absorbed light triggers photochemical changes in the chromophore. These changes are relayed to the protein as structural changes and the biochemical activity of the protein is modified, thereby passing the signal on.\nIn this thesis, time-resolved X-ray solution scattering has been used together with molecular dynamics simulations to probe the conformational dynamics of photoreceptor proteins. The investigations reveal both the sequence and nature of light-induced structural transitions. Diverse mechanisms of signal transduction on different length- and timescales were found, from the nanometer scale light-induced separation of domains in phytochromes, to the Ångström scale opening of the light-oxygenvoltage\ndimer and subsequent supercoiling of the linker region, to the sub Ångström changes in the radius of gyration of cryptochromes. The results provide a structural link between the early photochemical events and the interaction and regulation of downstream processes and proteins.

abstract: The retinal projections of the shark Scyliorhinus canicula were re-examined using the radioautographic method following the intraocular injection of tritiated tracers. New primary visual centers were identified. Overall 12 distinct sites of termination of contralateral optic endings were found distributed within five levels of the brain (hypothalamus, thalamus, pretectum, tectum and mesencephalic tegmentum). Furthermore the presence of a small ipsilateral retinal projection was demonstrated attaining the hypothalamic thalamo:pretectal and tectal levels. These new data broaden our understanding of the organization of the primary visual system in Scyliorhinus as defined previously using the degeneration technique.

abstract: The velvet belly lanternshark (Etmopterus spinax) is a small deep-sea shark commonly found in the Eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean Sea. As other members of the Etmopteridae family, it displays thousands of tiny epidermal light organs called photophores, which are composed of a cluster of photogenic cells (photocytes) enclosed in a pigmented sheath and topped by a shutter-like structure and a lens. These organs produce a blue-green light that is believed to be involved in numerous functions including camouflage by counterillumination, intraspecific communication and aposematism. According to recent pharmacological studies, this functional versatility is partly achieved thanks to a complex photophore control mechanism, which involves hormones and neural agents. Current experimental data suggest (i) photocytes and the shutter to be the main targets of these pharmacological substances, and (ii) the presence of a link between the targets since the shutter appears to open while photocytes are glowing and inversely. Here, we hypothesize extraocular opsins to endowe photophores with their own light perception (as it was recently shown in a bioluminescent squid) and hence to provide the link between shutter opening and photocyte activity. The present work uses various techniques including transcriptome analysis western blotting, immunohistochemistry to detect the presence of opsins in the shark’s photogenic tissue. Results confirm the presence of extraocular opsins associated with the photophores, which likely supports their involvement in the bioluminescence control mechanism.

eLasmobranc Dataset: An Image Dataset for Elasmobranch Species Recognition and Biodiversity Monitoring
abstract: Elasmobranch populations are experiencing significant global declines, and several species are currently classified as threatened. Reliable monitoring and species-level identification are essential to support conservation and spatial planning initiatives such as Important Shark and Ray Areas (ISRAs). However, existing visual datasets are predominantly detection-oriented, underwater-acquired, or limited to coarse-grained categories, restricting their applicability to fine-grained morphological classification. We present the eLasmobranc Dataset, a curated and publicly available image collection from seven ecologically relevant elasmobranch species inhabiting the eastern Spanish Mediterranean coast, a region where two ISRAs have been identified. Images were obtained through dedicated data collection, including field campaigns and collaborations with local fish markets and projects, as well as from open-access public sources. The dataset was constructed predominantly from images acquired outside the aquatic environment under standardized protocols to ensure clear visualization of diagnostic morphological traits. It integrates expert-validated species annotations, structured spatial and temporal metadata, and complementary species-level information. The eLasmobranc Dataset is specifically designed to support supervised species-level classification, population studies, and the development of artificial intelligence systems for biodiversity monitoring. By combining morphological clarity, taxonomic reliability, and public accessibility, the dataset addresses a critical gap in fine-grained elasmobranch identification and promotes reproducible research in conservation-oriented computer vision. The dataset is publicly available at https://zenodo.org/records/18549737.

Machine‐assisted image analysis facilitates conservation of iconic elasmobranchs
abstract: Abstract Photo‐identification (photo‐ID) is commonly used in wildlife ecology and management, but its effectiveness depends on reliable determination of whether an observed individual is already contained within the database. This is typically done by trained human operators but becomes an increasingly demanding task as photo‐ID databases expand, potentially limiting the method's applicability. Artificial intelligence approaches have been suggested as potential solutions to this problem. We present a case study involving a photo‐ID database of flapper skate ( Dipturus intermedius ) from Scotland, which was used to train a multistage, deep learning model using a method similar to high‐performing facial recognition system, FaceNet, to enable automatic assessment of the similarity between flapper skate newly submitted to the database and those pre‐existing in the database. Evaluation using a blind test set of 100 images taken from the database and also a second, smaller test set of tagged animals of known identity to confirm the model's photo‐ID performance for end users. When assessed against the previously unseen test set, the model achieved a mean average precision (mAP) of 84.1% and a top‐1 accuracy of 80%. The resulting photo‐ID model was integrated into the photo‐ID database, which was further tested with images of tagged individuals of known identity. This integration significantly reduced the time required to confirm whether new skates were already included in the database. With a top‐1 accuracy of 80%, the matching skate, if contained in the database, will likely be returned as a match, removing the need to check by eye against 2500+ individuals already in the database. Solution . The integration of machine‐assisted image analysis into a photo‐ID database of skate improved our ability to track individuals and understand movement and residency at far larger scales, essential for the continued management of the species. This approach is suitable for a wide range of research projects reliant on photo‐ID and should be considered for new and legacy data sets.

abstract: To provide precise configuration reference for the engineering bionics, high accuracy detection in large field of view on the natural biological body is a prerequisite. Targeting the streamline body of carcharhinus brachyurous, 3D (three dimensional) measurement was carried out with monocular and binocular vision inspecting system based on sinusoidal structure light. By means of moving the vision sensor driven by a stepper motor, fringe patterns with variable fringe spacing were projected to every parts of the shark body, then the point clouds of different parts of the whole shark body were obtained. title: Australian endangered species: Northern River Shark
abstract:
The Northern River Shark (Glyphis garricki) is one of the rarest species of shark in the world. It is known only from a small number of locations in Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Papua New Guinea. Discovered in Australia in 1986, only 36 specimens have been recorded here since. 
 
The Northern River Shark is a 2.5-3 metre long shark belonging to a family known as whaler or requiem sharks. Its closest relative in Australia is the Speartooth Shark, also found in northern rivers and estuaries and listed as Endangered by the IUCN. Distinguishing between the two is difficult, but is based on the location of the “waterline”, the point where the darker upper-body colouring of the shark changes to lighter lower colour. 
 
The eyes of the Northern River Shark are also unusually small, and are probably not relied on for finding prey. Instead, the Northern River Shark possess a relatively large concentration of ampullae of Lorenzini. These organs allow the shark to sense the electric fields of other organisms, and find them in the turbid rivers where the shark lives.

abstract: This working document presents the results on the most abundant elasmobranch species captured in the 2020 Spanish Groundfish Survey on Northern Spanish shelf. Biomass, spatial distribution and length ranges were analysed for Scyliorhinus canicula (lesser spotted dogfish), Galeus melastomus (blackmouth catshark), Etmopterus spinax (velvet belly), Raja clavata (thornback ray), Raja montagui (spotted ray), Leucoraja naevus (cuckoo ray) and other scarce elasmobranches. In general the biomass of these species remained high this last survey, despite the slight decline observed on S. canicula (lesser spotted dogfish), R. clavata (thornback ray) and R. montagui (spotted ray). A few specimens of the scarce elasmobranches Scymnodon ringens (knifetooth dogfish), Dalatias licha (kitefin shark), E. pusillus (smooth lanternshark), R. undulata (undulate ray) and L. circularis (sandy ray) were found as usual in this last survey whereas the occasional species Mustelus mustelus (smooth-hound), Neoraja iberica (iberian pygmy skate), Dipturus nidarosiensis (norwegian skate) and R. microocellata (small-eyed ray) were not. Gaelorhinus galeus (tope shark), Tetronarce nobiliana (electric ray), Dipturus oxyrinchus (longnosed skate), Torpedo marmorata (marbled electric ray) and Raja brachyura (blonde ray) were captured again since time ago in the time series and Centroscymnus crepidater (longnose velvet dogfish) was found for the first time in the historical series. Signs of recruitment were found for G. melastomus, G. atlanticus, R. clavata and L. naevus.

abstract:
Sharks are known to have the ability to detect weak electric field generated by its prey. The Ampullae of Lorenzini (AOL), first discovered by Stefano Lorenzini in 1678, has been identified as the biosensor which is responsible for electroreception. Since then, many experiments were conducted to determine the AOL’s functions. 
 
In this report, readings were done to gather the AOL sensitivity, functions, limitations and its principle of sensing prey. Individual components of the AOL system were considered in obtaining the main function and working of the shark’s AOL. 
 
With this knowledge in hand, a computer modeled prototype of an artificial AOL was created using Solidworks to mimic the AOL’s ability to detect the bioelectricity produced by the prey. One such application for the artificial sensor is mounting the sensor in ROVs and AUVs to detect presence of marine life in dark water conditions. Given sufficient time and resources, the design can be fabricated and implemented in these underwater crafts.
